title: Bayesian Learning of Distance Metrics Beyond RMSD for Biomolecule Alignment, Clustering, and Domain Identification
abstract: Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is the standard metric of structural comparison in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. In its conventional form, RMSD assigns equal weight to all atoms regardless of mobility. Hence, flexible loops and disordered regions can dominate a global RMSD, while the rigid functional core contributes negligibly to the overall metric. To address this issue, we introduce the Bayes-optimal RMSD (BRMSD), which optimizes per-atom weights jointly with structural averages by maximizing a Bayesian posterior. In a trade-off between low RMSD and weight uniformity, a position-fluctuation parameter $σ$ controls the transition from classical RMSD ($σ\to \infty$) to a progressive focus on a rigid core ($σ\to 0$). The BRMSD framework supports analysis modules for structural alignment, focused alignment onto a user-specified domain, trajectory smoothing, soft $K$-means conformational clustering, and rigid-domain identification. These modules are implemented in the open-source Python package BRMSD (https://github.com/bio-phys/BRMSD) and benchmarked on two MD systems, the endoplasmic reticulum translocon-associated protein SND3 and the phosphotransferase adenylate kinase.
summary: This paper develops the Bayes-optimal RMSD (BRMSD) metric to overcome the limitations of standard structural comparison metrics for biomolecules. By optimizing per-atom weights using a Bayesian framework, BRMSD effectively down-weights highly flexible regions and concentrates analysis power on the stable, rigid functional core of proteins. This provides robust tools for alignment, clustering, and domain identification in molecular dynamics simulations.
main_problem: Standard RMSD fails for biomolecules because it weights all atoms equally, allowing flexible regions to dominate the metric while ignoring rigid functional cores.
main_result: The proposed Bayes-optimal RMSD (BRMSD) significantly reduces structural deviation metrics compared to standard RMSD on benchmark systems like SND3. It successfully identifies and focuses analysis on the stable, rigid core of proteins.
method: The authors introduce a Bayesian framework that optimizes per-atom weights by maximizing a posterior derived from minimizing an effective free energy functional combining Mean-Square Deviation (MSD) and relative entropy regularization.
model_or_system: The methods are applied to biomolecules studied via Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, specifically benchmarking on the SND3 translocon protein and adenylate kinase. The framework is designed for structural alignment, clustering, and domain identification within these systems.
key_observables: BRMSD value, per-atom weights ($w_\alpha$), cluster responsibilities ($q(a|i)$), and the Calinski–Harabasz (CH) index for clustering quality.
important_parameters: The position-fluctuation parameter $\sigma$ controls the weight suppression threshold; parameters like $\mu/	heta$ control domain focusing strength, and window size $W_{op}$ is used for trajectory smoothing.
main_assumptions: Minimizing the free energy functional $G$ may only yield a local minimum, necessitating multiple random restarts. The method assumes that weight optimization can effectively separate rigid core contributions from flexible noise.
figures_summary: Figures show BRMSD significantly lower than standard RMSD over time; they also illustrate the anticorrelation between high-RMSF residues and low optimized weights, confirming domain identification via weight concentration.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the BRMSD framework by defining the free energy functional $G$. It then details specialized modules for focused alignment (adding a concentration penalty), trajectory smoothing (using windowed sums), soft K-means clustering (introducing responsibilities), and rigid domain identification (via sequential peeling).
why_interesting: While primarily applied to biophysics, the underlying mathematical machinery—optimizing weights based on local fluctuation statistics via free energy minimization and entropy regularization—shares conceptual links with statistical mechanics approaches used in analyzing complex many-body systems or disordered materials.
